- If sentiment is consistently negative (0.00) in recent history, model tends to overestimate; correct by reducing forecast slope or adding downward bias.
- If sentiment is positive (1.00) and model shows upward trend, model often over-optimistic; cap forecast growth or introduce early mean reversion.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >80), model frequently overshoots in next 5–10 days; apply lagged correction or reduce momentum in forecast.
- When true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 days of sharp drop after peak), model fails to adjust; add decay factor or use moving average smoothing.
- If sentiment history shows increasing positive sentiment (e.g., 0.25, 0.33), model often underestimates volatility; increase forecast variance or add upward bias.
- For 30-day horizon, model often underestimates late-period volatility; adjust last 5–7 days of forecast to be more volatile or higher mean.
- If sentiment is neutral (0.00) and model shows steady upward trend, model often misses downward correction; add early downward bias or use sentiment-triggered pivot.
